title: Designing a cancellation flow that is honest
metaTitle: An honest way to let people cancel
excerpt: Let people cancel from the billing page. Tell them what they keep and what they lose before they confirm. A maze of offers is a reason to dispute the charge and not return.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper, a cancellation path drawn so a person can see the way out.
caption: A flow sketched with user goals. Let them cancel, and say what they keep. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Where should a cancel button live?
faqs.answer: On the billing or account page, next to the plan, with the verb in the label. If a customer can upgrade without help, they should be able to find the exit without a search. Email and chat can be support. They should not be the only door on a self-serve plan.

faqs.question: What should the page say before someone confirms?
faqs.answer: What they keep, what they lose, and the dates, including the last day they will be charged and what happens to teammates. Repeat those facts in the confirmation email. A surprise at the exit is the same failure as a surprise cost at checkout.

faqs.question: Is it acceptable to offer a pause or a cheaper plan?
faqs.answer: One relevant offer is fair if the cancel control is just as easy to see and use. Do not chain a pause, a discount, and a required survey before the door. Ask a skippable question after the cancellation has already succeeded, if you ask at all.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Let a customer cancel. Tell them what they keep and what they lose, before they confirm. A cancellation flow ux that hides the button, loops them through offers, or saves nothing until they beg is a maze. The maze is a reason to dispute the charge. It is also a reason not to come back when they need you again.

The honest version is short. Find the control. See the consequences. Confirm. Get a record. Offer a real alternative only if it is a real alternative, and never as a wall.

## Put the control where the account lives

The cancel action belongs with the plan, the billing page, or the account settings. The same place they went to upgrade. A person who can buy in two clicks should be able to find the exit without a search. Label it with the verb. "Cancel plan." "Close account." A label that says "Manage" and then hides the verb one layer deeper is the maze, one step early.

Do not make the only path an email to a founder, a chat that is offline, or a phone line with hours they cannot meet. Those can exist as help. They cannot be the only door. If your product has a self-serve upgrade, it needs a self-serve exit. If the plan was sold by a person and the contract says a person must close it, say that on the billing page, with the address and what to include. Silence is not a policy. It is a scavenger hunt.

Write the words in the product, not only in a help article. People will not read the help article first. They will look at the billing page, fail to find a verb, and then get angry. Nielsen Norman Group's note on the opening seconds applies inside the product too. A page that does not show its purpose quickly gets abandoned, or, in this case, escalated. Show the verb.

Hanabi's product work, including interfaces like Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai, treats a scannable control as the point. Cancellation is a scannable control with consequences. It should look like the rest of the product. Same button logic. Same plain language. A special dark pattern page with a different type system tells the customer that this moment is where you stop being the company you claimed to be.

## Say what they keep and what they lose

Before the confirm button, list both. Keep: the export, the data until a date, the right to reopen, the projects that stay readable. Lose: the paid features, the extra seats, the custom domain, the integrations that depended on the plan. Dates matter. "Read-only until 30 June, then the workspace closes" is a fact. "You'll lose access" is a threat with no calendar.

Say what happens to other people. Teammates, clients who had a login, a connected store. The person clicking may not be the only person affected. If they are about to strand a colleague, the page should say so while there is still time to warn them. This is not a guilt trip. It is information the clicker often does not have in working memory.

Say what happens to money. The last day they are charged. Whether the current period is refundable. Whether a pause exists. If you do not refund the period, say that in the list, not in a tooltip. Baymard Institute's checkout research is about the other end of the money path, and the lesson still travels: surprise costs and missing totals are why people abandon and why they get angry. A surprise at the exit is the same failure in reverse. Show the total consequence before the confirm.

Repeat the list in the confirmation email, in the same words. The email is the record they will need if a charge appears later. A cute subject line and a different set of facts will not help them, or you, in a dispute. Plain subject. The date. What ended. What remains.

## One offer, then the door

You may make one relevant offer. A pause. A cheaper plan that still does the job they came for. A shorter export window extended if they need it. The offer has to be something you would defend as useful, not a coupon designed to exhaust them.

Show the offer, and show the door beside it. "Pause for a month" and "Cancel now" can share a screen. The cancel control must be as easy to see as the offer. A bright offer and a text link in low contrast is the maze wearing a smile. The WCAG overview groups the standard under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. An exit that fails contrast, or that cannot be reached by keyboard, fails the person who is already frustrated. Make the exit operable.

Do not chain offers. A pause screen, then a discount screen, then a survey wall, then a "are you sure" that resets the form, is a chain. One offer. One confirm. If they say no to the offer, the next thing they see is the confirmation, not a second pitch.

A survey can exist after the cancel has succeeded, and it can be skippable. Ask one question. Use the answers. A required essay before the door is not research. It is a toll. If you truly need a reason for your own learning, ask it when the exit is already done, and accept silence.

Do not shame the copy. "We're sorry to see you go" is optional and fine if it is one line. "Why would you abandon your team" is a pressure tactic. You can be warm and still let them leave. Warmth is a tone. It is not a series of dialogs.

## Confirm, record, and stop charging

The confirm button repeats the verb and the date. "Cancel on 30 June." A button that says "Submit" is how misclicks happen. After it, show a success state that restates the keep-and-lose list and the email they should expect. The success state is part of the design, not a toast that vanishes.

Stop the charge when you said you would. The flow is a lie if the billing system does not match the sentence. This is the unglamorous half of the work, and it is the half that creates disputes. Design, engineering, and the person who owns billing should walk the same path on a staging account before you ship. Submit it. Check the email. Check the next invoice. Check the access on the end date, not only on the day you clicked.

Give them a receipt they can find later inside the product. A billing history line: canceled, the date, the plan that remains. People lose email. The product should remember. A Hanabi-built product would treat that history as a state of the account, designed with the empty and the canceled states, not as an afterthought in an admin tool only your team can see.

If something fails, say so and say what to do. "We could not cancel. You have not been charged again. Write to us at this address." A spinner that ends in the same screen, with the plan still active and no explanation, will send them to their bank. You will then spend more time on the dispute than the honest flow would have taken.

## Coming back, and the people who stay

Say whether they can return, and what return means. Same data, if it is still there. A new trial, if it is not. The price they will pay if the price changed. A customer who left cleanly is a possible customer later. A customer who left angry is a story they tell. You do not need a win-back campaign inside the cancel flow. You need an exit that does not manufacture the anger.

Do not delete their export early because you are tidying the database. If you promised ninety days, keep ninety days. Write the job down where the on-call engineer will see it. A promise on the screen is a requirement.

For the people who do not cancel, the flow should be invisible. Do not show a tragic banner to the rest of the company because one admin looked at the page. Do not email the whole workspace "someone tried to leave" as a pressure leak. The actor is the admin. The consequences you listed are the right audience for the news.

Read the flow once a quarter. Click it yourself, on a phone, on the production-like account. Products rot at the exit because teams love the entrance. The entrance gets the new illustration. The exit gets a broken style from two redesigns ago. Bring the exit along when the type changes. It is part of the product's voice.

Figma is the right place to draw the states: offer, confirm, success, failure, already-canceled. Framer can help you feel whether the chain is too long. The build, in React and TypeScript, should use the same components as the rest of billing. A one-off cancel page is how the contrast slips and the focus ring disappears.

## The trial is the other exit

A trial that ends by locking the work, with no date given in advance, teaches the same lesson as a maze. The customer learns not to trust the next screen. Cancellation is the paid version of that moment. The trial needs its own plain speech: the date, what stops, and how to continue.

Do not use the cancel flow as a substitute for explaining the trial, and do not use a trial-end lockout as a substitute for a cancel button. They are different days. A person on a trial may never have a plan to cancel. A person on a plan may have already paid. Speak to the day they are actually in.

If your notes and your billing page disagree, fix the notes. A release note that says "you can leave whenever you want" and a billing page with no verb is the kind of contradiction QA should catch before a customer does. The piece on [trial endings that do not feel like a trap](/blog/trial-endings-that-do-not-feel-like-a-trap) is the next read if the anger you are seeing starts before the first invoice.

When you want a second pair of eyes on an exit that has grown too many steps, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the billing screen and the email the customer gets. The useful outcome is a shorter path: what they keep, what they lose, and a door that works.
